passage: "Suraj, you're teaching Class 4 now, so listen to your old Vaibhav Chacha for a minute. Years ago I had a boy in my class, bright as a lamp. Around Diwali he changed. He snapped at his friends over nothing. He put his head on the desk every afternoon. He stopped playing kabaddi, which he used to love, and every week he said his stomach hurt. The other teachers said, 'Cranky phase. He'll grow out of it.' But it didn't pass. Weeks, then two months. One day I asked him gently, 'What's it like inside, these days?' He said, 'Grey, Sir.' Just that. Grey. I called his parents that same evening, and they took him to a doctor who helped. Children don't say 'I feel low,' Suraj. They show it. Watch for the change that stays."

qa.q: What game did the boy stop playing?
qa.a: Kabaddi, which he used to love.

qa.q: What did the boy's answer 'Grey, Sir' reveal about how he felt?
qa.a: It revealed that he felt low and flat inside, even though he had only shown it as crankiness and tiredness.

qa.q: What choice did Vaibhav Chacha make after the boy said 'Grey, Sir', and why did it matter?
qa.a: He called the boy's parents that same evening instead of waiting for a phase to pass, and that led to a doctor who helped.

qa.q: How did the other teachers see the boy's behaviour, and why was that risky?
qa.a: They saw a cranky phase he'd grow out of, which could have left his lasting sadness unnoticed.

grounding: An elder recalls a child whose low mood showed as crankiness, tiredness, lost interest in play and stomach aches, and a lasting change that got attention.

passage: With the new baby home and both parents on night shifts at the hospital, nobody had much time for Nirmala, ten. The flat was full of crying and tired whispers. When Rashmi Masi came to help, she noticed at once. Nirmala snapped at her little cousin over a pencil. She lay on the sofa after school, too tired to change. Her dance bag hadn't moved from the corner in weeks. Twice she said her head hurt. "She's just jealous of the baby," her mother sighed. But Rashmi sat with Nirmala on the balcony and asked, "Is everything a bit heavy lately?" Nirmala nodded and cried silently. That night Rashmi told her sister, "This has gone on too long to be a phase." The next day, between shifts, they took Nirmala to the doctor together.

qa.q: Where had Nirmala's dance bag been lying?
qa.a: In the corner, not moved in weeks.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when Rashmi asked about things being heavy?
qa.a: She felt low and relieved to be asked; she nodded and cried silently.

qa.q: What choice did Rashmi make that changed things?
qa.a: Instead of accepting it as jealousy, she gently asked Nirmala, then told her sister the lasting change needed a doctor.

qa.q: How did Nirmala's mother see the behaviour, and why?
qa.a: She saw it as jealousy of the baby, perhaps because she was exhausted from night shifts and caring for the newborn.

grounding: It shows a child whose low mood looks like crankiness, tiredness, tearfulness, lost interest and aches, with a relative noticing a lasting change that deserves attention.

passage: For most of the term, Vaibhav, ten, had been different in class. He snapped at his bench partner over a borrowed eraser. He put his head on the desk after lunch and said his head hurt, then his stomach. At games he sat on the steps instead of playing football, which he used to love. When Sangeeta Ma'am asked him to read, he muttered, "Why do I always have to?" and his eyes filled. After class she didn't scold. She sat beside him. "You've seemed tired and cross for weeks. That's not like you. Is something heavy?" He shrugged. "Everything's just boring." Sangeeta called his parents that afternoon and asked the school counsellor to meet the family that week.

qa.q: What sport did Vaibhav use to love?
qa.a: He used to love football.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav's snapping and tears suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest he was feeling low and sad inside, even though he could only say that everything was boring.

qa.q: Why was Sangeeta Ma'am's response wise?
qa.a: She noticed the change had lasted weeks, asked gently instead of scolding, and involved his parents and the counsellor that same day.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav's bench partner see him lately?
qa.a: The bench partner might see Vaibhav as grumpy or mean, without knowing he may be struggling with sadness.

grounding: Shows a child whose low mood appears as crankiness, tiredness, tears, aches and lost interest in play, and a teacher who treats the lasting change seriously.

passage:
Early June: Farhan, nine, stopped going up to the roof to fly kites with his cousins. "Boring," he said, and lay on the sofa. Farida, his Ammi, thought it was the heat.
Two weeks later: He cried over a lost pencil and shouted at his little sister for humming. Every morning he said his stomach hurt. He was asleep by seven.
The next week: Farida sat on his bed. "Jaan, you've been cross and tired for a long time now. What does it feel like inside?" Farhan thought. "Heavy. Like I'm carrying a bag." The next morning she took him to the paediatrician, who listened carefully and suggested they also see a child counsellor.

qa.q: What did Farhan stop doing in early June?
qa.a: He stopped going up to the roof to fly kites with his cousins.

qa.q: How did Farhan describe what he felt inside?
qa.a: He felt heavy and sad, like he was carrying a bag, though he had shown it only as crossness and tiredness.

qa.q: What did Farida do once she saw the change had lasted?
qa.a: She asked him gently how it felt inside and took him to the paediatrician the next morning, who suggested a child counsellor.

qa.q: How might Farhan's little sister have experienced his shouting?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and confused, not understanding why her brother was suddenly so cross.

grounding: Shows a child whose sadness shows as irritability, tears, tiredness, aches and lost interest, and a parent who notices the lasting change and gets help.

passage: "Baljeet puttar, you've been snapping at everyone this month, na? Come, let your Dadu tell you something. When I was ten, after we moved to Ludhiana, I became a real grump. I kicked the door, I shouted at my brothers, I said my legs hurt so I wouldn't have to play gulli-danda. I slept in the afternoons. Everybody said Harish has become badtameez. But my Bebe saw it had gone on for months. She took me for a walk to the canal and asked, 'Are you missing the old house?' I burst into tears. I didn't have words like sad. I only knew I was cross. She took me to our family doctor and spoke to my teacher too. So, puttar, how are you feeling, really?"

qa.q: Where did Harish's family move when he was ten?
qa.a: They moved to Ludhiana.

qa.q: What was young Harish really feeling behind his grumpiness?
qa.a: He was sad and missing the old house, but he had no words for it, so it came out as crossness.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Harish?
qa.a: His Bebe noticed the change had lasted months, gently asked about the old house, and then took him to the family doctor and spoke to his teacher.

qa.q: How did the people around young Harish see his behaviour at first?
qa.a: They thought he had become badtameez, rude, not realising he was sad.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood sadness that showed as irritability, aches and lost interest, noticed as a lasting change by his grandmother, who got help.

passage:
The family was moving flats that month, and the house was all boxes, drilling and shouting. At first nobody noticed much about Noor, ten.
But Bhavna Masi, staying to help pack, did. Noor snapped at her little cousin over nothing. She lay on the sofa after school instead of going down to play cricket, which she used to beg for. She said her tummy hurt most mornings and cried when her pencil broke.
"She's just cranky from the move," Noor's father said, carrying a box.
"It's been three weeks," Masi said quietly. "She's stopped drawing too."
That night Masi sat on Noor's bed. "You seem heavy lately. Like a rain cloud." Noor's lip shook. "I don't know. I just don't want to do anything."
The next morning Masi and Noor's parents sat down together and booked a visit to the family doctor.

qa.q: What did Noor used to beg to go and do?
qa.a: Play cricket downstairs.

qa.q: How was Noor feeling underneath the crankiness?
qa.a: She seemed sad and low but couldn't say so, which came out as snapping, tiredness, tears and tummy aches.

qa.q: What did Bhavna Masi do well?
qa.a: She noticed that the change had lasted weeks, gently asked Noor about it and got the parents to book a doctor's visit instead of blaming the move.

qa.q: How might Noor's father have seen things before Masi spoke up?
qa.a: He was busy and stressed with the move and saw Noor as simply cranky, not as a child who was quietly struggling.

grounding: Noor seems cranky, tired and tearful, stops playing and has aches, and her aunt treats the lasting change as something that deserves attention.
